meta.title: A Hardware-Aware Comparison: Keypoint vs. End-to-End Pose Estimation for Space Objects
meta.authorsHtml: Andreas Rebsamen<sup>1</sup>, Matthias Hoefflin<sup>1</sup>, Andreas Ming<sup>1</sup>, Juergen Wassner<sup>∗</sup><sup>1</sup>

abstract: Vision-based pose estimation enables autonomous spacecraft navigation but faces two major challenges: domain gaps between synthetic training images and real sensor data, and tight resource constraints of space-qualified hardware. This paper presents a hardware-aware comparison of keypoint-based and direct end-to-end 6D pose estimation approaches for space objects, evaluating pose accuracy and runtime on an FPGA accelerator. To study domain gaps, we test on raw rendered images and Camera-inthe-Loop datasets that introduces realistic optical, sensor, and processing effects. Quantized keypoint-based models achieve on average 48 % lower pose estimation error than end-to-end models, at the cost of 1.6× to 10× longer runtime. A robustness-optimized end-to-end architecture, obtained via evolutionary architecture search, increases robustness to domain shifts while maintaining a competitive accuracy–runtime trade-off. We also demonstrate that parameter count and FLOPs alone are insufficient runtime indicators, since architectural design and accelerator characteristics strongly influence runtime.

blocks.html: The growing congestion of low Earth orbit (LEO) risks rendering it unusable without active debris removal [1]. This has spurred substantial research into vision-based navigation (VBN) using monocular pose estimation from a single onboard camera for chaser satellites.

In this paper, we systematically compare two convolutional neural network (CNN)-based approaches to pose estimation: direct end-to-end regression and keypoint prediction with a Perspective-n-Point (PnP) post-processing. The survey by Pauly et al. [2] provides a comprehensive overview of pose estimation for space objects, discussing various works including those using SPEED [3] or SPEED+ [4] datasets. However, results remain difficult to compare due to inconsistent training conditions, datasets, and the fact that each study typically analyzes only one of the two approaches.

Moreover, deployability on space-qualified hardware has received little attention. Metrics like parameter count or FLOPs are sometimes reported, but offer limited insight into runtime or energy consumption [5]. While [6] lists various field programmable gate array (FPGA)-based accelerators for space applications, FPGA-accelerated pose estimation exists only for keypoint approaches [7].
Given these shortcomings, the main contributions of this paper are:
• To the best of our knowledge, this is the first systematic comparison of end-to-end and keypoint models trained under identical conditions on the same dataset.
• We present results on model robustness under the domain gap introduced by a real-world vision sensor and an FPGA-based image processing pipeline.
• We analyze end-to-end model behavior for difficult dataset cases.
• We provide real-time performance figures on a spaceready FPGA System-on-Chip (SoC) platform for all model architectures.
This section describes the experimental setup: model architectures, training, data sets, and evaluation metrics.

We use MobileNetV2 [8] and VGG16 [9] as CNN backbones for both approaches, ensuring comparable network architectures for end-to-end and keypoint approach. The general principle of the model architectures are illustrated in Figure 1 and detailed further below.

In the end-to-end architecture, global average pooling (GAP) is used to flatten the CNN backbone output. Three subsequent fully connected layers produce a 7-element output vector representing the full 6D pose: three position coordinates and a four-dimensional rotation quaternion.

Additionally, we extend the end-to-end experiments with a custom architecture discovered via evolutionary architecture search (EAS) [10]. EAS jointly minimized pose error and multiply-accumulate (MAC) operations, bounded by parameter count. Top models were analyzed for robustness to quantization and input perturbation. The most robust was selected for this study.

In the keypoint architecture, the CNN backbone serves as encoder, connected to a CNN decoder comprising five transposed convolution layers that generate 10 keypoint heatmaps at the same spatial resolution as the input image. Feature maps from each decoder upsampling block are concatenated with corresponding encoder feature maps, as shown in the right part of Figure 1.

A subsequent argmax layer extracts 2D keypoint locations, which are considered valid if the maximum exceeds 0.25. In a post-processing step, pose coordinates are recovered from valid keypoints with a PnP solver, in our case solvePnPRansac from the OpenCV library [11].

All models were trained using TensorFlow 2.14 [12]. For both approaches, several pixel-based input augmentations were applied. Following fp32 training, the models are fine-tuned using three additional epochs of quantization-aware training (QAT) with the TensorFlow Model Optimization Toolkit (TF-MOT), which applies quantization wrappers that insert fake-quantization operations to simulate 8-bit quantization while preserving gradient flow.

Positions are encoded in normalized device coordinates (NDC), with x and y as normalized image coordinates in [−1, +1]. The z coordinate in meters is similarly normalized to [−1, +1] via min −max scaling. For orientation, the model directly regresses quaternion components. This uniform output range across all values simplifies quantization with consistent scaling.

For the training loss, the NDC position vector [X, Y, Z] is converted to coordinates in meters p = [Xm, Ym, Zm] using camera intrinsics and a pin-hole model. The position loss Lp is the mean squared error (MSE) between groundtruth p and predicted position ˆp:
The orientation loss Lo uses the squared dot product distance for normalized quaternions, where θ denotes the relative rotation angle:

The joint loss balances Lp and Lo, which operate on different scales, using the homoscedastic uncertainty formulation from [13]. The loss weights are estimated as task variance ˆs := log(ˆσ2), added as regularization term against infinite uncertainty and learned to improve numerical stability. Since the orientation loss does not constrain quaternion norms, we add Lon = 1 −||ˆq||2 to enforce unit quaternions. Despite not required for fp32 inference, a deterministic output range is beneficial for quantization. The total loss, with αn = 0.1 in our experiments, is:

blocks.html: Keypoints are defined in Blender using farthest point sampling (FPS) [14, 15]. The target object mesh is loaded and the algorithm iteratively selects 10 vertices on the mesh, starting with the one furthest from the object origin. Subsequent keypoints are selected to maximize inter-keypoint distances.

For label generation, each keypoint is projected onto the image plane, generating a 2D Gaussian heatmap centered at its coordinates. The Gaussian peaks at 1.0 and decays to 0.5 at a 5-pixel distance. During training, the MSE loss between the predicted and ground-truth heatmaps is minimized.

Training uses 2 million synthetic images of Sentinel-6 [16] generated in Blender. The target object is scaled to a length of 1.5 m and uniformly distributed 3–20 m away within the field of view, illuminated by a single light source from random directions.

The test set combines 4480 simulated R-bar approach images with 647 random poses for diversity. Two versions are used: RAW (unaltered Blender renders), and CIL (Camerain-the-Loop), where renders are displayed on an OLED monitor and re-captured by the camera pipeline featuring an IMX334 sensor [17], introducing domain gap from monitor and sensor distortions, seen Figure 2, left. Additionally, extreme samples are held out for separate evaluation. A sample qualifies as extreme if:

Left: End-to-end design with global average pooling (GAP) and dense layers outputting seven pose coordinates directly. Right: Keypoint-based design with skip connections between CNN encoder and decoder, ending in an ArgMax layer for 2D keypoint coordinates.

We evaluate fp32 and int8 models (int8 directly from QAT including fake-quantization operations) on both RAW and CIL test sets using three metrics: mean absolute error (MAE) for position based on Equation (4); mean orientation error (MOE) based on the quaternion angular distance in Equation (5); and the mean pose error combining relative position and orientation in Equation (6), as defined in [3].

blocks.html: Each int8 model is compiled for a VectorBlox V1000 [18] accelerator and executed on an MPFS250TS PolarFire FPGA-SoC [19]. Per-frame inference time is measured in hardware. For reference, we additionally report the number of parameters and FLOPs for each model.

Table 1 summarizes model results on normal and extreme samples. Section 3.1 compares keypoint vs. end-to-end state-of-the-art (SOTA) CNN. Section 3.2 benchmarks SOTA end-to-end models against our EAS architecture.

Additional results for larger input resolution, omitted here for reasons of space, show the expected reduction in pose estimation error with a substantial runtime penalty, and otherwise confirm the findings in this work.

Cols. 1–2 vs. 3–4 in Table 1 show keypoint models outperforming end-to-end models on normal samples, especially in orientation estimation. The overall pose error on the CIL datasets is reduced by 57 % and 39 % for int8 MobileNetV2 and VGG16, respectively. This aligns with findings in [2, 3] that geometric constraints reduce error.

Keypoint models fail to deliver valid results on extreme cases. This behavior provides explicit failure signals, a valuable feature in safety-critical applications. End-to-end models always output estimates without uncertainty indications. However, cols. 6–8 show that their estimates typically exceed random guessing even for extreme inputs.
Keypoint models show superior robustness to CIL-induced domain gaps (MAE rows), suggesting they better capture domain-independent geometric features.

Col. 3 shows that CIL fp32 consistently underperforms, and position MAE exceeds random guessing. Unlike keypoint models or VGG16 end-to-end, MobileNetV2 end-to-end fails to bridge the domain gap despite heavy training augmentations. Interestingly, quantized versions succeed, with QAT serving as effective robustness augmentation.
The higher parameter count explains VGG16’s superior CIL robustness, both in keypoint and end-to-end models.
FPGA runtime does not scale linearly with parameters or FLOPs. This can be seen for both backbones, where execution time rises disproportionately.

For MobileNetV2 and VGG16, the runtime of the keypoint models is 10× and 1.6× longer, while FLOPs increase by 6.2× and 1.1× and parameter count by 1.5× and 1.3×, respectively. A potential cause are the additional external memory transfers needed for more complex networks and for skip-layer intermediates in keypoint models.

blocks.caption: CIL test set samples. Left: Two normal samples revealing the sharp discrepancy between high-fidelity renders typical of existing high-resolution VBN datasets and realistic hardware-captured images. Right: Two extreme samples where the target occupies only few pixels.

blocks.html: In this subsection we compare SOTA CNNs against our EAS-optimized architecture.

While the EAS architecture does not outperform the others on the RAW test set, it is able to outperform MobileNetV2 for CIL and exhibits less degradation than VGG16 going from RAW to CIL or from fp32 to int8. Thus, the EAS architecture, which was deliberately selected for robustness, trades higher pose estimation error on normal samples for superior robustness.
On extreme samples, the int8 EAS model even outperforms both SOTA models on the CIL test set.

The runtime of the EAS architecture falls between the two SOTA architectures. Although it exceeds VGG16 in parameter count, it runs much faster in hardware, reinforcing that parameter count alone poorly predicts real-time performance.
This study evaluates keypoint-based versus direct end-to-end regression for 6D pose estimation of space objects.

Keypoint approaches yield superior average accuracy but exhibit total failures on extreme cases, while end-to-end models deliver reasonable estimates even then. Advanced post-processing (e.g., Gaussian curve fitting on heatmaps) could boost keypoints and cut invalid rates. However, raw heatmaps reveal prediction quality via valid keypoints or Gaussian shapes. End-to-end lacks such uncertainty cues.

Keypoint methods improve robustness against domain shifts. The choice of architecture independently affects robustness, as demonstrated by our EAS-optimized custom model. Systematic architecture search can enable tailored trade-offs in runtime, accuracy, and robustness.

FPGA real-time benchmarking revealed end-to-end throughput advantages, but keypoint models exhibit lower normal-case estimation error. Furthermore, we showed that parameter count and FLOPs correlate only weakly with runtime, which is governed by hardware details and model-accelerator interplay.

Future work will extend EAS to keypoint models and incorporate Hardware-in-the-Loop (HIL) testing for FPGA-specific optimization, evaluate models on standardized datasets, and enhance keypoint performance via advanced heatmap post-processing.
